On 10 March 1952, less than three months before a presidential election, General Fulgencio Batista seized power in Cuba in a nearly bloodless coup. He took over army barracks at dawn, and President Carlos Prio fled. Batista cancelled the vote.

He had ruled Cuba in the 1930s as an army strongman, and was elected president from 1940 to 1944. Polls showed him far behind in 1952, which is thought to have pushed him to act. The United States recognised his government within weeks.

Opponents went to court first. A young lawyer and candidate for parliament named Fidel Castro filed a petition arguing that Batista had broken the constitution. It was ignored. Castro concluded that the system could not be changed by law, and on 26 July 1953 he led an attack on the Moncada barracks.

Batista's second period of rule, a harsh dictatorship friendly to US business and organised crime, ended on 1 January 1959, when he fled in the face of the Cuban Revolution.
